extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent prosecution attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating asserted utility, evidentiary burdens, and claim interpretation during patent examination under 35 U.S.C. 101, including special considerations for therapeutic/pharmacological inventions and the PTO's claim construction standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of truth for applicant's asserted utility
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification disclosure that teaches how to make and use the invention in terms corresponding in scope to the claimed subject matter must be taken as complying with the enabling requirement, and the Office should presume a statement of utility made by an applicant is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should not begin by questioning the truth of the statement of utility; instead ask whether there is any reason to question it. Evaluate the logic of the applicant's statements and any evidence cited. If the asserted utility is credible (i.e., believable based on the record or the nature of the invention), a rejection for lack of utility is not appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard — preponderance of the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: To overcome the presumption of truth for an applicant's asserted utility, Office personnel must establish that it is more likely than not that one of ordinary skill in the art would doubt the truth of the statement of utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The evidentiary standard throughout ex parte examination is a preponderance of the totality of the evidence; a preponderance exists when it suggests the asserted statement is more likely than not false. Office personnel must provide evidence sufficient to show that the statement would be considered false by a person of ordinary skill, using both facts and reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an asserted utility is not credible
rubrics_metrics.description: An asserted utility is not credible only when (A) the logic underlying the assertion is seriously flawed, or (B) the facts upon which the assertion is based are inconsistent with the logic underlying the assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credibility refers to the reliability of the statement based on logic and facts offered by the applicant. Do not label inventions or therapeutic claims 'incredible' or 'speculative' as a starting point; 'incredible utility' is a conclusion reached only after evaluating applicant assertions and evidentiary basis. Rejections have been sustained where applicant failed to disclose any utility or asserted a utility contradicting scientific principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial burden on the Office — prima facie showing and evidentiary support
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office must (A) make a prima facie showing that the claimed invention lacks utility, and (B) provide a sufficient evidentiary basis for factual assumptions relied upon in establishing the prima facie showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO must do more than merely question operability — it must set forth factual reasons that would lead one skilled in the art to question the objective truth of the statement of operability. If the Office cannot develop a proper prima facie case and evidentiary support, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 should not be imposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie showing elements for lack of specific and substantial utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the asserted utility is not specific or substantial, a prima facie showing must establish that it is more likely than not that a person of ordinary skill would not consider the asserted utility to be specific and substantial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prima facie showing must contain: (A) an explanation clearly setting forth the reasoning used to conclude the asserted utility is neither specific nor substantial nor well-established; (B) support for factual findings relied upon; and (C) an evaluation of all relevant evidence of record, including utilities taught in the closest prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie showing elements for lack of specific and substantial credible utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the asserted specific and substantial utility is not credible, a prima facie showing must establish it is more likely than not that a person skilled in the art would not consider credible any specific and substantial utility asserted by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prima facie showing must contain: (A) an explanation clearly setting forth the reasoning used to conclude the asserted utility is not credible; (B) support for factual findings relied upon; and (C) an evaluation of all relevant evidence of record, including utilities taught in the closest prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie showing when no specific and substantial utility is disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: If no specific and substantial utility is disclosed or well-established, a prima facie showing of no specific and substantial utility need only establish that applicant has not asserted a utility and that, on the record before the examiner, there is no known well-established utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must use specificity in setting forth an initial rejection so the applicant can identify and address the Office's assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity requirement in initial rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: It is imperative that Office personnel use specificity in setting forth an initial rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 and support any factual conclusions made in the prima facie showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using specificity helps the applicant identify assumptions made by the Office and properly address them in rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner evidentiary requests to substantiate an asserted utility
rubrics_metrics.description: In appropriate situations, the Office may require an applicant to substantiate an asserted utility for a claimed invention when operativeness appears unlikely or the alleged utility appears incredible in view of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When requesting evidence, the examiner should indicate why the factual record is defective relative to applicant assertions and, where appropriate, specify what type of evidentiary showing can remedy the defect. Requests for additional evidence should be imposed rarely and only if necessary to support scientific credibility of the asserted utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on demanding additional test data
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO should not demand further test data when such data would be essentially redundant or unduly burden the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only after the PTO provides evidence showing one of ordinary skill would reasonably doubt the asserted utility does the burden shift to the applicant to provide rebuttal evidence. Examiners should avoid requesting redundant evidence and should be mindful of precedent cautioning against undue burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's response and burden shift
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proper rejection has been imposed, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut the prima facie showing using amendments, arguments, or new evidence (e.g., affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.132, or printed publications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New evidence must be relevant to the issues raised. Declarations that set forth conclusions without establishing a nexus to supporting evidence, or that merely express opinions, may be of limited probative value. Office personnel must review original disclosure, evidence relied on in the prima facie showing, claim amendments, and any new reasoning or evidence, and must recognize, consider, and respond to each substantive element of the applicant's reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of evidence related to utility — no fixed quantity/character
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no predetermined amount or character of evidence that must be provided to support an asserted utility; the amount and character will vary depending on what is claimed and whether the asserted utility contravenes established scientific principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants do not need to prove utility beyond a reasonable doubt or with statistical certainty. Evidence is sufficient if, considered as a whole, it leads a person of ordinary skill in the art to conclude the asserted utility is more likely than not true. Courts have reversed rejections where applicants provided reasonable evidentiary support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable correlation for therapeutic/pharmacological utilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of pharmacological or other biological activity will be relevant to an asserted therapeutic use if there is a reasonable correlation between the activity and the asserted utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant can establish reasonable correlation with statistically relevant data, arguments/reasoning, documentary evidence (e.g., scientific articles), or any combination. The applicant need not prove correlation with statistical certainty or provide human clinical success; only a reasonable correlation is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural similarity as supportive evidence for therapeutic utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of close structural similarity to a compound known to have a particular therapeutic utility can support an assertion of therapeutic utility for a new compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should evaluate not only the existence of structural relationship but also the reasoning offered to explain why structural similarity is relevant. Structural similarity combined with evidence of activity (e.g., animal models) should be given appropriate weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: In vitro and animal testing generally sufficient for therapeutic utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Data from in vitro assays or animal models, if reasonably correlated to the asserted therapeutic utility, will generally be sufficient to establish therapeutic or pharmacological utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must evaluate factors influencing a skilled artisan's conclusions, including test parameters, choice of animal or composition, relationship of activity to the disorder treated, and the applicant's explanation of why the data supports the asserted utility. Lack of an industry-recognized animal model is not dispositive if one skilled in the art would accept the tests as reasonably predictive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human clinical data not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should not impose the burden of providing evidence from human clinical trials to establish therapeutic utility; there is no decisional law requiring human clinical data to demonstrate utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an applicant has initiated human clinical trials, the Office should presume the applicant has established that the subject matter of those trials is reasonably predictive of the asserted therapeutic utility. But absence of human data is not, by itself, a basis for rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and efficacy are outside PTO patentability review
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office must confine its review to the statutory requirements of the patent law and should not require evidence of safety in human treatment or the degree of effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other agencies (e.g., FDA) handle safety/effectiveness standards. While FDA review may provide persuasive rationale, FDA approval is not a prerequisite for finding usefulness under the patent laws. In challenging utility, the Office must carry its burden even if the FDA or other experts have approved a rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of claims for difficult or previously untreatable diseases
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to treating or curing diseases for which there have been no previously successful treatments warrant careful review; credibility of asserted utility may be harder to establish where contemporary understanding suggests the task is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The absence of a known cure does not automatically mean lack of utility. An assertion that treats a symptom may require modest support; an assertion of 'curing' may require significantly greater evidence. Affidavit evidence from experts indicating a reasonable expectation of success, supported by sound reasoning, usually should be sufficient to establish credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be given their broadest reasonable interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: During patent examination, pending claims must be given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO determines scope of claims not solely on claim language but 'in light of the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.' Because applicants can amend claims during prosecution, applying the broadest reasonable interpretation reduces the possibility that an issued claim will be interpreted more broadly than justified. Examiners should avoid importing limitations from the specification into the claim that have no express basis in the claim language.
